references.text: David instructs his men to greet with peace ("Shalom") when they enter a house, reflecting the same greeting of peace that Jesus commands the disciples to give.
God declares "Peace, peace" over those who are far and those who are near. This is the background for the messianic greeting of peace that Jesus sends his disciples out with.

Jesus gives similar instructions to the twelve disciples to greet a house with peace when they enter, and that the peace should return to them if the house is not worthy. Parallel passage to Luke 10:5-6.
Continuation of the verse: If a child of peace is there, let peace rest on him; if not, let it return to the disciples.
Jesus gives similar instructions at the sending out of the twelve: they are to stay in the house they enter. The same pattern for missionary practice.
The Aaronic blessing includes that the Lord shall give peace, which forms the basis for the biblical practice of blessing with peace.
The psalmist prays for peace over Jerusalem and wishes peace within its walls and prosperity in its strongholds – the biblical tradition of wishing peace over a place and its inhabitants.
Paul ends the letter with an exhortation to greet one another, saying "the God of peace be with you" – the apostolic practice of the greeting of peace reflecting Jesus' commission.
Peter ends the letter with "Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace be with all who are in Christ." The greeting of peace in the early church has its root in Jesus' instruction in Luke 10:5.
